blocks.text: Assyrian royal annals and the Lachish reliefs provide independent primary evidence for the crisis behind this chapter, but they are not neutral, complete reports of the campaign. The annals claim the capture of fortified Judahite cities, deportations, Hezekiah's confinement in Jerusalem, territorial redistribution, and tribute delivered at Nineveh. Their failure to claim Jerusalem's capture is significant, yet silence by itself cannot establish how the city survived in Isaiah's account. The differing rhetoric and sequence invite readers to distinguish Assyrian royal self-presentation from a full reconstruction of events.

The Assyrian evidence anchors Sennacherib, Hezekiah, Judah, Jerusalem, fortified cities, and tribute in the 701 BCE crisis, while also showing why the chapter should not be read as though either account were a neutral transcript. Its royal claims and commemorative choices provide a distinct perspective alongside Isaiah's portrayal of the confrontation.

A six-sided baked-clay prism, written in Akkadian with Sennacherib's royal annals, records his campaign against fortified Judahite cities and his treatment of Hezekiah. It independently connects the Assyrian king, Hezekiah, Judah, tribute, and the 701 BCE campaign with the narrative setting of Isaiah 36–37, while its royal perspective keeps it from functioning as a neutral transcript of the biblical account.

Elsewhere in Isaiah's Assyrian-era material, reliance on foreign coalitions and military resources is challenged, and trust in YHWH is presented as a political as well as a religious issue. That wider concern helps frame the pressure in Isaiah 36–37: Sennacherib's demand is not only a military threat but also a challenge to Judah's trust.

sections.title: The Crisis in Its Wider Setting
